- 3163.TWO Browave: Another Taiwan supplier with exposure to FAUs, passive optical components, and WDM connectivity, positioning it around the fiber-interface bottleneck.

- $GLW Corning: Probably the broadest U.S.-listed beneficiary of the fiber side. Corning has exposure to optical fiber, fiber arrays, fiber-to-PIC connectivity, bend-insensitive fiber, and fiber-management solutions, allowing it to address multiple bottlenecks simultaneously.

tweets.text:
The line that immediately caught my attention:

"800VDC AI data centers launch in 2027: SiC and GaN become the power backbone."

At first glance, this looks like a $NVTS / GaN / SiC story.

But the more I look at it, the bigger opportunity may be the entire AI power delivery value chain.

-

Why 800VDC?

As AI racks move toward MW-scale power, 48V/54V becomes increasingly difficult because current gets enormous.

At 1MW:

54V → ~18,500A
800V → ~1,250A

Higher voltage dramatically reduces current, easing constraints around copper, busbars, connectors, conduction losses, and heat.

So 800VDC is not just about efficiency.

It is increasingly an architectural requirement for MW-scale AI racks.

-

And this is much broader than SiC and GaN.

The power chain increasingly looks like:

Grid AC → 800VDC → 48V / 12V / 6V → <1V XPU

SiC and GaN become critical in the high-voltage conversion stages, but the final challenge is still delivering thousands of amps at sub-1V directly into the GPU/XPU.

That creates another major bottleneck.

-

This is why I think $MPWR deserves much more attention here.

$MPWR has exposure not only to high-density power conversion, but also to multiphase Point-of-Load power around GPUs and CPUs.

Potentially:

800V → intermediate voltage

and

intermediate voltage → XPU core

Two different layers of the same AI power stack.

-

$VICR is an even more interesting architecture bet.

As GPU power moves into the multi-kW range while core voltage remains below 1V, even the final few centimeters of power delivery become problematic.

This is where Vertical Power Delivery becomes interesting.

Instead of feeding power laterally across the board, power can be delivered vertically, directly underneath the XPU.

As compute density keeps rising, reducing PDN impedance and losses at the package level could become increasingly important.

-

The architecture is also not fully settled yet.

We could see:

800V → 48V
800V → 12V
800V → 6V

Different vendors are pursuing different approaches.

So I currently think of them as:

$MPWR → relatively architecture-agnostic exposure

$VICR → higher-beta bet on 48V + Vertical Power Delivery

$NVTS → more direct pure-play exposure to GaN-based high-voltage conversion

-

SiC and GaN themselves also serve different roles.

SiC
→ higher voltage
→ high power
→ protection
→ front-end conversion

GaN
→ high-frequency switching
→ high power density
→ compact DC/DC conversion

This may not be a winner-takes-all market.

They can occupy different parts of the same AI power architecture.

-

The upstream side may be even more interesting.

A 2027 800VDC rollout does not mean SiC/GaN yield challenges suddenly disappear.

Before large-scale deployment, the industry still needs progress in:

200mm wafer migration
epitaxy defect reduction
yield improvement
reliability qualification
capacity expansion

That opens another layer of beneficiaries:

SiC substrate / epi → $COHR, $WOLF
Ion implantation → $ACLS
Inspection / metrology → $KLAC
Power infrastructure → $VRT, $ETN

-

So I think framing this simply as:

“800VDC = Navitas”

is far too narrow.

The bigger picture is:

Grid → HVDC → SiC/GaN → DC/DC → Vertical Power Delivery → XPU

As AI rack power density keeps rising, the entire power delivery network needs to be redesigned alongside compute.

There may be far more beneficiaries here than the market currently associates with the 800VDC transition.

- $SNDK's HBF is better viewed as a new memory tier between HBM and NAND rather than an HBM replacement.

- HBF Grade 3 targets 512GB of capacity and up to 3.072TB/s of bandwidth.

- Its main advantage is roughly 8–16× more capacity than HBM at a similar cost.

- OXMIQ modeled HBF at roughly 14× the capacity of HBM but only about 60% of its aggregate bandwidth.

- HBF wins when model capacity is the bottleneck, while HBM remains superior for high-throughput token generation.

- The strongest HBF use cases are MoE expert weights, massive KV caches, and sparse long-context inference.

- More local capacity could also reduce expert parallelism and expensive GPU-to-GPU all-to-all traffic.

- The biggest hurdle is software, as GPU runtimes and frameworks such as vLLM would need explicit HBM-HBF data-placement support.

- The key takeaway is that HBF looks more like an expansion of tiered AI memory architecture than an "HBM killer," suggesting limited direct displacement of HBM for now.

Performance, Reliability and Manufacturability of 1060nm VCSEL Arrays for AI Datacenter Scale-Up

Same wavelength, same application. The new word is manufacturability. The first two get used at the research stage. The third one does not.

The materials angle is what matters here. VCSELs live on GaAs, not InP. A different substrate from the one that keeps getting named as the bottleneck of this AI optical cycle.

Which raises a question. If GaAs takes the ultra short reach of scale-up, where does the top of the InP demand curve stop. And for a company that sells both InP and GaAs substrates, which way does that substitution cut.

"Never in history."

Check out the value chain.

NVIDIA’s guidance points to something much broader than stronger GPU demand.

The key signal is that AI infrastructure bottlenecks are spreading across memory, packaging, networking, optics, power, cooling, grid capacity, and datacenter construction.

- Compute silicon: $NVDA, $AMD, $AVGO, $MRVL

- HBM / DRAM: $SKHY, $MU, Samsung Electronics

- Advanced packaging: $TSM, Amkor, ASE

- Semiconductor equipment: ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, Tokyo Electron

- Test / probe: $FORM

- AI networking: NVIDIA, Broadcom, Marvell, Arista Networks

- Optical transceivers / optical engines: $COHR, $LITE, $AAOI, Innolight

- InP / lasers: Lumentum, Coherent, $AXTI, Sumitomo Electric

- Silicon photonics / CPO: Marvell, Broadcom, $INTC, $TSM, $TSEM, $GFS

- Optical fiber / connectivity: $GLW, Fujikura, Furukawa Electric, Sumitomo Electric

- Networking systems / DCI: Arista Networks, Cisco, Nokia, $CIEN

- High-density power conversion: $VICR, Monolithic Power Systems

- Datacenter power infrastructure: Vertiv, Eaton

- Cooling: Vertiv, Modine, Schneider Electric

- Grid infrastructure: GE Vernova, Eaton, Quanta Services

- Power generation: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Constellation Energy, Vistra, Cameco

- Datacenter construction: Quanta Services, EMCOR, Comfort Systems

- Datacenter / powered land: Equinix, Digital Realty and hyperscalers

- Storage / memory disaggregation: Marvell, Micron, $SNDK and the CXL ecosystem

The chain can be simplified to:

GPU → HBM → Packaging → Networking → Optics → Fiber → Power Delivery → Cooling → Grid → Generation → Powered Land

The important takeaway is that the beneficiaries of AI infrastructure spending are moving increasingly farther away from the GPU itself.

Memory constraints:

SK hynix / Micron → HBM equipment and test → advanced packaging

Power and datacenter constraints:

Vertiv / Eaton / GE Vernova / Quanta Services / Comfort Systems → grid capacity and powered land

Larger AI clusters:

Arista Networks / Marvell / Broadcom → Lumentum / Coherent → Corning → Ciena

And this is where silicon photonics and CPO become increasingly important.

NVIDIA’s revenue growth itself does not prove silicon photonics adoption.

The stronger argument is that continued AI growth increases cluster size, bandwidth requirements and rack power density, pushing electrical interconnects closer to their physical limits.

That creates increasing pressure to move toward optical I/O, CPO and eventually scale-across architectures.

AI is no longer just a semiconductor buildout.

It is becoming a memory, networking, optics, power and physical-infrastructure buildout.

I love this kind of question because it gets to the fundamental physics behind the technology, and ultimately the engineering consequences.

According to the paper by $SKHY, the difference in total power is already substantial. For an 800 Gbps link, the authors estimate 3.1–5.3 W per end for a microLED-based transceiver, versus 9.8–12 W per end for mainstream laser-based active optical cables, a 56–68% reduction.

So the thermal implication could be important as well.

<InP laser-based architecture>

electricity
→ high-power CW laser
→ laser conversion loss and heat
→ temperature-dependent wavelength drift
→ wavelength stabilization / potentially TEC
→ additional power
→ additional heat

<microLED-based architecture>

electricity
→ many low-power, directly modulated emitters
→ no lasing-threshold requirement
→ no wavelength locking required for a spatially parallel architecture
→ potentially eliminates or reduces high-speed SerDes, DSP, and FEC overhead
→ much lower total link power
→ potentially much lower system-level thermal load

The important point is not simply that a microLED itself “runs cooler” than an InP laser. It is that the entire link architecture can become simpler and consume much less power, which then reduces the heat that has to be removed.

And once optics sits next to compute and HBM, that second-order effect could become just as important as the pJ/bit number itself.
